question: As at 31 December 2023, the Italian cement sector had received 55 393 187 EUAs (European Union Allowance). Worth around EUR 4.5 billion, they had been allocated during Phases II and III of the Emissions Trading System (ETS).

Yet, pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2023/956, authorised declarants who import goods subject to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and operate in the same market as those producing the emissions will, as of January 2026, have to purchase CBAM certificates with their own resources. The introduction of CBAM will run in parallel with the gradual reduction of free allowances under the ETS.

However, while importers were never allocated any free allowances, emission producers were, and will also be able to surrender the ones their excess EUAs. This state of affairs has resulted in an imbalance which will, in the short term, have critical consequences for companies and stakeholders in the sectors subject to CBAM.
If no legislation is enacted to remedy this situation, the introduction of CBAM be fatal to many small and medium-sized enterprises. In the light of above: 1.
Has the Commission realised that the allocation of excess free allowances has distorted competition in many markets?
Has the Commission considered other ways of implementing the CBAM that would remedy the distortions caused by the above allocations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2025) 1. The existence of free allocation exceeding emissions in the first phases of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is well known, especially between the years 2008 and 2012, but to a lesser extent also in later years.

This situation was addressed already with measures taken following the revision of the ETS Directive1 in 2018, strengthening the system, and a shortage of free allocation compared to verified emissions can clearly be seen from the start of the fourth trading period in 2021.

It should also be highlighted that the majority of excess allowances are assumed to have been sold, and to a fraction of the value quoted, since the current value of an EU Allowance is more than 10 times higher than 10 years ago. Hence, the Commission does not see a major risk of distortion of competition. 2.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)2 obligation to be paid by importers will be reduced by the corresponding free allocation that an EU producer would receive for the production of the same goods. This will ensure that products produced in the EU and in third countries are treated equally.

This adjustment for free allocation will include a definition of CBAM benchmarks, which in turn will be based on a combination of the EU ETS benchmarks. The gradual phase-out of ETS free allowances in CBAM sectors from 2026 to 2034 will be mirrored by a corresponding increase in the CBAM obligation.
This is because the CBAM adjustment for free allocation will gradually decrease and thereby the CBAM obligation will increase.
1 Directive (EU) 2018/410 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 March 2018 amending Directive

2003/87/EC to enhance cost-effective emission reductions and low-carbon investments, and Decision (EU) 2015/1814 (OJ L 76, 19.3.2018, p. 3, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2018/410/oj 2 Regulation (EU) 2023/956 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 establishing a carbon border adjustment mechanism (OJ L 130, 16.5.2023, p. 52, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/956/oj
